findings.title: Mixed import styles in synthesize.py
findings.description: synthesize.py uses both 'import X as alias' and 'from X import Y' styles for importing from scripts modules. Lines 14 and 16-18 use 'import ... as', while line 15 uses 'from ... import'. This inconsistency makes the module's dependencies less clear and reduces readability.
findings.impact: Reduced code clarity and consistency. Makes it harder to track what external symbols are being used and their origins.
findings.remediation: Choose a single import style for scripts module imports and apply consistently.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly against the source. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py lines 14-18 read exactly: line 14 'import scripts.citations as citations', line 15 'from scripts.citations import load_cwe_catalog', line 16 'import scripts.evidence as evidence_mod', line 17 'import scripts.html_report as html_report', line 18 'import scripts.ingest_tools as ingest_tools'. The claim's factual assertion (line 14 and 16-18 aliased-module style, line 15 from-import style) is literally correct, and the block is preceded by the sys.path.insert at line 13 that makes the 'scripts.*' package importable. The inconsistency is not merely cosmetic: the SAME module, scripts.citations, is imported twice by two different mechanisms, and the same symbol is then reached two different ways within the file -- line 600 calls the bare 'load_cwe_catalog()' while line 923 calls 'citations.load_cwe_catalog()'. Both styles even appear inside a single function body: line 600 'catalog = load_cwe_catalog()' sits twenty lines above line 620 'citations.enrich_citations(findings, catalog, epss_enabled=False)'. I checked for a functional justification for the line 15 duplicate and found none. A repo-wide grep for 'load_cwe_catalog' shows the only consumers are scripts/citations.py:37 (the definition), synthesize.py:15/600/923, and tests/test_citations.py, which imports the function from the citations module itself (cit.load_cwe_catalog) and never from scripts.synthesize -- so line 15 is not a compatibility re-export. Contrast this with the deliberate, commented re-export at synthesize.py:24 ('load_json_tolerant = evidence_mod.load_json_tolerant'), whose docstring explicitly states it exists to keep the name importable as scripts.synthesize.load_json_tolerant for existing callers/tests; no such justification exists for line 15. A grep for 'monkeypatch' and 'setattr(' across the repo returned no matches, so no test patches scripts.citations.load_cwe_catalog in a way that would require one binding style over the other (note that if such a test were ever added, the two call sites would behave differently -- line 923 would see the patch, line 600 would not, which is a latent trap the mixed style creates). Peer modules mostly pick one style per file, though the codebase is not uniform overall (scripts/tools/legacy_sarif.py:5-6 mixes the same two styles, while scripts/run_tools.py and scripts/tools/__init__.py use from-import consistently); the project's own plan docs at docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-03-epistemics-core.md:691 instruct contributors to 'Match the file's existing import style', which is a soft in-repo convention supporting the finding. Severity LOW is appropriate -- this is a readability/consistency defect with no correctness or security impact, and remediation is a one-line change (drop line 15 and make line 600 call citations.load_cwe_catalog(), matching line 923). One correction to the claim: the attached citation CWE-1104 (Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components) is mis-assigned and unrelated to import style; the accurate mappings are CWE-1076 (Insufficient Adherence to Expected Conventions) and its parent CWE-710 (Improper Adherence to Coding Standards). The claim's 'verified: false' flag on CWE-1104 is consistent with it being unvalidated.

findings.title: sys.path manipulation undermines module installability
findings.description: Multiple scripts manipulate sys.path to enable local imports (line 10 in _run_adapter.py, line 13 in synthesize.py, line 11 in run_tools.py, line 9 in dispatch.py). This pattern prevents the code from being cleanly installed as a package and relies on execution context.
findings.impact: The codebase cannot be installed via standard Python packaging tools. Brittle when run from different directories. Makes containerization and deployment more complex. IDE tooling struggles with import resolution.
findings.remediation: Convert the project to a proper Python package with pyproject.toml. Use relative imports or add the package to PYTHONPATH during installation. Remove all sys.path.insert() calls.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: All four cited locations are verbatim accurate at the exact line numbers given: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py:10, synthesize.py:13, run_tools.py:11 (all three inserting the skill root via os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))), and dispatch.py:9 (inserting the scripts dir itself). The pattern is broader than the claim states: two more production modules do it (skill/scripts/tools/base.py:9, skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:11), roughly 30 test modules replicate it, and the CI workflow itself bootstraps the same way inline (.github/workflows/security.yml:58 does sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.getcwd(), 'skill')) before 'import scripts.ingest_tools'). The installability premise holds on inspection. A pyproject.toml does exist at the repo root, which initially looked like it would refute the claim, but it contains only [project] metadata and [tool.ruff] config -- there is no [build-system] table and no setuptools/hatch package-discovery configuration, so the project declares no build backend and is not a buildable/installable distribution today. Consistently, the entire skill tree contains exactly one __init__.py (skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py); there is no skill/__init__.py and no skill/scripts/__init__.py, so the 'scripts' package resolves only as a PEP 420 namespace package rooted at whatever directory the sys.path.insert supplies. 'scripts' is also a very generic top-level name that would be collision-prone in site-packages. Beyond style, there is a concrete demonstrable defect the claim does not name: the import roots are inconsistent. dispatch.py:9 inserts the scripts directory and imports flat ('import depth_planner', 'import model_resolver'), while synthesize.py/run_tools.py/_run_adapter.py insert the skill root and import qualified ('import scripts.citations', 'from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS'). The test suite mirrors both conventions (tests/test_depth_planner.py 'import depth_planner' vs tests/test_evidence.py 'import scripts.evidence'). Any process that loads both roots gets the same source file registered under two distinct sys.modules identities, yielding duplicated module-level state and identity/isinstance checks that can silently disagree. Two sub-clauses of the stated impact are, however, wrong and should be corrected before this is actioned. (1) 'Brittle when run from different directories' is false for the cited production lines: every one of them derives from os.path.abspath(__file__), which is cwd-independent; only the CI snippet uses os.getcwd(). (2) 'Makes containerization and deployment more complex' is contradicted by the in-code rationale at _run_adapter.py:7-9, which documents that the sys.path insert is precisely what lets the module import identically under the container's /src mount and on a developer host -- here it simplifies containerization rather than complicating it. Net: the core architectural assertion (pervasive sys.path manipulation, no working packaging, imports resolved by an ad hoc bootstrap rather than installation) is verified; the severity rests on the unstated assumption that pip-installability is a goal for what is distributed as a vendored/copied agent skill, which the repo does not establish. Confidence is LIKELY rather than CERTAIN for that reason and because part of the impact narrative is demonstrably inaccurate.

findings.title: Fragile sys.path manipulation at module import time
findings.description: sys.path manipulation occurs at module level before subsequent imports (_run_adapter.py line 10, dispatch.py line 9, run_tools.py line 11, synthesize.py line 13). This pattern is duplicated across 4 files and relies on sys.path.insert succeeding silently. If insertion fails or sys is unavailable, the subsequent 'from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS' statements will fail with confusing ImportError messages.
findings.impact: Fragile import mechanism could mask real errors and make debugging difficult. Duplicate code creates maintenance burden. Not idempotent if modules are re-imported.
findings.remediation: Centralize sys.path manipulation in a single module initialization function or use proper package structure with __init__.py files. Alternatively, configure PYTHONPATH at the execution level rather than module level.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The factual predicate is verified verbatim at every cited location: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py:10, dispatch.py:9, run_tools.py:11, synthesize.py:13 each perform a module-level sys.path.insert before subsequent imports. The claim actually UNDERSTATES the duplication: a repo-wide grep finds 6 sites, not 4 — skill/scripts/tools/base.py:9 and skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:11 use a third variant (os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, os.pardir)). There are also two semantically different variants in play: _run_adapter/run_tools/synthesize insert the PROJECT ROOT and then do package imports ('from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS'), while dispatch.py:9 inserts the SCRIPTS DIR itself at sys.path[0] and imports bare top-level names ('import depth_planner', 'import model_resolver'), which additionally creates a top-level module shadowing surface. The claim's description conflates these by attributing the 'from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS' consequence to dispatch.py, which does not contain that import.

Supporting evidence the original reviewer did not cite, which strengthens the structural core: (1) there is NO skill/scripts/__init__.py — the only __init__.py in the tree is skill/scripts/tools/__init__.py, so 'scripts' resolves as a PEP 420 namespace package while 'scripts.tools' is a regular package, exactly the incoherent packaging the remediation targets. (2) skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py carries a '#!/usr/bin/env python3' shebang yet has NO sys.path bootstrap and no __main__ block, while doing 'from scripts.tools.sarif_utils import (...)' at line 13. It resolves only because its importer (synthesize.py:18) already mutated sys.path first. That is a genuine, currently-latent import-order dependency: invoking it directly, or importing it before synthesize, raises ImportError. (3) skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py's own docstring states it 'exists to break the circular import between scripts.ingest_tools' and the adapters — the team has already paid refactoring cost to untangle this graph, which directly substantiates the claimed maintenance burden.

However, the claim's stated FAILURE MECHANISMS are materially wrong and should not survive into the report: 'relies on sys.path.insert succeeding silently' and 'if insertion fails' describe a non-existent failure mode (sys.path is a list; list.insert cannot fail here); 'or sys is unavailable' is nonsense since sys is a builtin; and 'not idempotent if modules are re-imported' is incorrect because module-level code executes once per interpreter via sys.modules caching, and even in the double-import-under-two-names case duplicate sys.path entries are harmless. The real fragility is packaging incoherence, cwd/entry-point sensitivity, and the ingest_tools ordering dependency — not silent insert failure.

The bootstrap itself is deliberate and functional: run_tools.py:167 invokes '/opt/panopticon/scripts/_run_adapter.py' inside the container while SKILL.md documents host invocation as 'python3 scripts/dispatch.py', i.e. two different roots, which is why the shim exists. So this is a maintainability/structure defect, not a broken code path — consistent with the finding's 'structure' category and MEDIUM severity (arguably LOW-MEDIUM).

Citation correction: CWE-427 (Uncontrolled Search Path Element) is a mis-citation and I do not endorse it. Every inserted path is derived from os.path.abspath(__file__), fully program-controlled, with no attacker-influenced env var, cwd, or relative element. There is no security weakness here; the appropriate mapping is a code-quality CWE such as CWE-1041 (Use of Redundant Code). CONFIRMED on substance, confidence LIKELY rather than CERTAIN because only the duplication/maintainability half of the claim survives scrutiny while the asserted impact mechanism does not.

findings.title: Panel-review lens-coverage fallback text conflates two opposite dispatch states
findings.description: In build_plan(), `non_spawned = [lens["name"] for lens in panel_lenses if lens["name"] not in spawned_set]` is empty in two semantically opposite situations: (a) the profile defines no lenses at all for this panel, where the panel reviewer genuinely must cover everything itself, or (b) the profile defines lenses but every one of them was spawned as a dedicated lens_sweep agent, where the panel reviewer should cover NONE of the mechanical lenses. Both cases render the same fallback string: `"\n".join(...) or "- (all lenses)"`. This is directly observable in this very run: scout-._5.json defines exactly one lens for the architecture panel which fully spawns at depth=standard, so dispatch-plan-._5.json has `"lenses": []` for the architecture panel_review entry, yet the rendered prompt says '- (all lenses)' — telling the reviewer to cover everything when a dedicated lens_sweep-architecture agent already ran. The same collision reproduces across this session's other dispatch plans (._1, ._4, ._6, ._7, ._10).
findings.impact: Panel reviewers are systematically told to 'cover all lenses' in exactly the case where a dedicated mechanical lens_sweep agent already covered them, causing redundant duplicate review work (wasted token budget, duplicate findings that then rely on dedupe/reinforce to reconcile) instead of being told to focus purely on holistic/cross-cutting concerns. Because this triggers for any panel whose lens set size is <= the depth's spawn limit, it is not a rare edge case but reproducible, always-on behavior for that configuration.
findings.remediation: Distinguish the two empty-non_spawned cases explicitly before building the fallback string: use '- (no additional lenses — all covered by dedicated lens sweep agents)' when panel_lenses is non-empty but non_spawned is empty, and reserve '- (all lenses)' only for the case where panel_lenses itself is empty.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Verified directly in source and in generated artifacts. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/dispatch.py line 253 computes `non_spawned = [lens["name"] for lens in panel_lenses if lens["name"] not in spawned_set]`, and line 274 renders `"lenses": "
".join("- %s" % n for n in non_spawned) or "- (all lenses)"`. Python's `or` on an empty joined string collapses BOTH empty-list causes to the identical literal, exactly as claimed: (a) panel_lenses empty, and (b) panel_lenses fully consumed by spawned_set. depth_planner.plan_lenses (skill/scripts/depth_planner.py) caps spawns at DEPTH_LIMIT {shallow:1, standard:2, deep:3}, so any panel whose lens count is <= that limit (with spawn=true and depth_threshold met) yields non_spawned == [] via case (b). Empirically reproduced: .panopticon/scout-._5.json defines exactly one architecture lens (name 'architecture', spawn true, priority 1, depth_threshold 'shallow') at depth 'standard'; .panopticon/dispatch-plan-._5.json line 298 has "lenses": [] for the architecture panel_review, its embedded prompt at line 300 contains the section '## Lenses assigned to this panel

- (all lenses)', and lines 303-310 of the same plan show a dedicated lens_sweep agent with "lens": "architecture" that already covers it. The collision is not an isolated artifact: `"lenses": []` appears 10 times across .panopticon/dispatch-plan-._1/._4/._5/._6/._7/._10.json, matching the claim's enumeration, and older rendered prompts show the same text (e.g. .panopticon.prev-20260803/prompts/06-._4-architecture.md line 13). The defect is structurally systemic rather than incidental because skill/agents/scout.md lines 52-62 prescribe single-lens defaults for the architecture and database panels ('architecture: architecture', 'database: database') and instruct spawn=true whenever a group has >=5 files or risk is high; therefore for a schema-conforming scout profile, case (b) is the normal steady state for those panels while case (a) (a panel with no lenses at all) is essentially never emitted, meaning the '- (all lenses)' string in practice fires almost exclusively in the semantically inverted situation. Contradiction inside the same prompt is confirmed too: skill/agents/panel-review.md line 16 tells the reviewer to 'Cover all lenses assigned to this panel that are NOT being handled by dedicated lens sweep agents', while the substituted {lenses} block (line 21) says '- (all lenses)'; the prompt never enumerates which lenses were spawned, so the reviewer has no data to resolve the contradiction and the most natural reading is to cover everything. Existing tests do not pin this behavior: tests/test_dispatch.py asserts only the non-empty cases (test_shallow_emits_only_panel_review expects ["style"], test_panel_review_includes_non_spawned_lenses expects ["novel"]); no test covers the empty non_spawned rendering, so the remediation would not break coverage. Two calibration notes for the auditor, neither of which negates the claim: (1) the impact is prompt-clarity/duplicated-effort (wasted tokens, duplicate findings pushed onto dedupe/reinforce), not a correctness or security failure - the machine-readable plan field "lenses": [] is correct and only the human/agent-facing rendering is ambiguous, so MEDIUM is at the upper end of defensible and LOW would also be reasonable; (2) the attached CWE-670 (Always-Incorrect Control Flow Implementation) is a poor mapping - control flow here is not incorrect, the defect is an ambiguous falsy-coalescing default in generated instruction text, and no security weakness class cleanly applies. The remediation as written (branch on `panel_lenses` being non-empty before choosing the fallback string) is correct and sufficient.

findings.description: AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS = ("source", "reinforced") strips only these two self-asserted trust fields from agent-authored finding JSON before synthesis (per the SEC-102 fix noted in the surrounding comment). findings.impact: A single agent-sourced finding can unilaterally claim independent cross-panel corroboration it never received. findings.title: Self-asserted corroborated/corroborated_by fields bypass agent-trust sanitization and forge cross-panel verification status
findings.description: `load_findings()` strips only `AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS = ("source", "reinforced")` (line 93; stripping loop at lines 125-129) from agent-authored finding JSON before it enters the pipeline. `corroborated` and `corroborated_by` — a field pair with the exact same trust-conferring character the code's own comment (lines 88-92) warns about — are not in that denylist. `evidence.derive_evidence()` (evidence.py:64-66) unconditionally trusts `finding.get("corroborated")`/`finding.get("corroborated_by")` when computing the authoritative `evidence.status`, and `evidence.triage_priority()` (evidence.py:81-84) gives a self-asserted `corroborated=true` the same priority boost as a genuine cross-panel match. The only code meant to set these fields, `synthesize.cross_panel_corroboration()` (synthesize.py:380-382), only ADDS the flag to findings that really do cluster with a different panel's finding within its 2-line window — it never clears a pre-existing self-asserted `true` on findings that fail to cluster. So a panel_review/lens_sweep agent's finding JSON that already carries `"corroborated": true` survives synthesis unchanged and is treated downstream as independently confirmed.
findings.impact: The forged status (a) inflates evidence_stats.corroborated and the human-facing corroborated marker in render_summary(), misrepresenting verification strength; (b) is used by triage_priority() to promote the finding to priority 0 in build_verify_queue() — the same tier as genuinely corroborated CRITICAL/HIGH findings. Under --max-verify N, a forged priority-0 entry can occupy an advisor-verification slot that would otherwise go to a real uncorroborated CRITICAL/HIGH finding (priority 1), which is then cut from the queue and left at evidence status unverified — outside GATE_ELIGIBLE_DEFAULT — so a genuine vulnerability can be excluded from grading/gate decisions. This directly violates the invariant evidence.py's own module docstring states: 'a reviewer cannot confirm its own finding.'
findings.remediation: Add "corroborated" and "corroborated_by" to AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS in synthesize.py so load_findings() strips them from every agent-authored payload before synthesis, identically to source/reinforced. Corroboration must then only ever be set by cross_panel_corroboration()'s own clustering pass, which already runs after stripping.

findings.title: html_report's compare fingerprint reimplements (and regresses) synthesize's already-fixed finding-identity logic
findings.description: synthesize.finding_fingerprint() (synthesize.py lines 515-534) deliberately excludes free-text `description` from its stable-identity hash, with the comment 'free-text description... agent prose is re-worded every run' — and the result is stored on every finding as f["fingerprint"] by build_report(). Separately, html_report.py's _fingerprint(), used exclusively by the --compare feature's _match_findings(), computes its own independent hash from [panel, category, file, title, description] — including the exact raw description text that synthesize's version was fixed to exclude for this precise reason — and never reads the already-computed finding.get("fingerprint") field that ships in every synthesized report.
findings.impact: synthesize.py --compare loads two already-synthesized report JSON files (each containing the correct, stable fingerprint per finding) but _match_findings() ignores that field and recomputes its own, reintroducing the non-determinism bug that finding_fingerprint() was written to solve. Any agent-sourced finding whose description is reworded between two runs of the same underlying issue will fingerprint differently in the compare view, and _match_findings() will report it as one 'resolved' entry plus one unrelated 'new' entry instead of 'unchanged' — corrupting exactly the delta counts and per-finding delta badges that --compare exists to produce.
findings.remediation: Have html_report._fingerprint() prefer the precomputed finding.get("fingerprint") (falling back to a local computation only for legacy reports that predate the field, and dropping description from that fallback to match synthesize.finding_fingerprint's rule_id/title discriminator).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every factual assertion in the claim verified verbatim against the code. (1) skill/scripts/synthesize.py:515-534 finding_fingerprint() builds its hash from [panel, category, normalized file, discriminator] where discriminator = tool_evidence.rule_id or title, with the docstring stating it 'Deliberately EXCLUDES line numbers (issues survive code moves) and free-text description (agent prose is re-worded every run).' (2) build_report() at synthesize.py:623 sets f['fingerprint'] = finding_fingerprint(f) for every finding in the loop at line 621, and line 681 returns 'findings': active — the same mutated dicts — so the field ships in every written report JSON (asserted by tests/test_synthesize.py:1599-1602 test_report_findings_carry_fingerprints). (3) skill/scripts/html_report.py:246-257 _fingerprint() independently hashes [panel, category, _normalize_path(file), title, description] — including the exact free-text description synthesize was fixed to exclude — and drops the rule_id discriminator entirely. (4) _match_findings() at html_report.py:260-289 calls _fingerprint(f) on both sides (lines 269, 272) and never reads finding.get('fingerprint'); grep for 'fingerprint' across skill/ shows the only reads of the stored field are none — html_report.py never references it. (5) The path is reachable and operates on already-synthesized reports: synthesize.py:861-887 handles --compare by json.load()ing two report files and calling html_report.write_html(report_b, html_out, compare_report=report_a), which reaches render() (html_report.py:683-692) and _match_findings at line 686. So two persisted reports that each carry a correct stable fingerprint have that field discarded and a description-sensitive hash recomputed. findings.title: Ad hoc sys.path bootstrap duplicated verbatim across three entry-point scripts
findings.description: synthesize.py (lines 13-18), run_tools.py (lines 11-13), and _run_adapter.py (lines 10-12) each independently execute `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))` immediately before `import scripts.<module>`, so that the `scripts` package resolves regardless of CWD. The same two-line idiom is copy-pasted three times rather than factored into one shared helper, and it hard-codes an assumption that each file lives exactly two directories below the importable root.
findings.impact: There is no single source of truth for how these scripts locate the `scripts` package; a future move of any one file (or a switch to installing skill/ as a real package) silently breaks that file's imports with a bare ModuleNotFoundError and no indication of the expected layout, and any layout fix must be applied in three places kept in sync by hand.
findings.remediation: Factor the bootstrap into one shared module (e.g. skill/scripts/_bootstrap.py) imported first by every entry point, or eliminate it by shipping skill/ as an installable package with `scripts` as a proper package.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly against the source. All three cited sites exist verbatim: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py line 13, skill/scripts/run_tools.py line 11, and skill/scripts/_run_adapter.py line 10 each contain the identical statement `sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))`, and each is immediately followed by package-qualified imports that depend on it (synthesize.py lines 14-18 `import scripts.citations/evidence/html_report/ingest_tools`; run_tools.py lines 12-13 `from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS` / `from scripts.tools.legacy_sarif import ...`; _run_adapter.py line 12 `from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS`). The cited line range 13-18 for synthesize.py is exact. A repo-wide grep for `sys.path.insert` confirms no shared bootstrap helper exists: skill/scripts/ contains no _bootstrap.py (globbed the directory listing), and there is no `skill/scripts/__init__.py` — `scripts` resolves only as a PEP-420 namespace package off the injected `skill/` root. pyproject.toml declares [project] metadata (name=panopticon, version 3.0.0) but has no [build-system] or package-discovery configuration, so `skill/` is NOT currently shipped as an installable package; the sys.path hack is the only import mechanism, confirming the claim's premise. The duplication is in fact broader than claimed and the 'no single source of truth' impact is understated: skill/scripts/tools/base.py line 9 and skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py line 11 use a semantically equivalent but textually different variant (`os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, os.pardir)`) to reach the same `skill/` root, while skill/scripts/dispatch.py line 9 uses a third, incompatible scheme (single dirname, then bare `import depth_planner`), and skill/scripts/ingest_tools.py line 13 does `from scripts.tools.sarif_utils import ...` with no bootstrap of its own, relying on whichever caller ran first. The hard-coded depth assumption is real: the two dirname() applications encode each file's position relative to the importable root (the container path /opt/panopticon/scripts/_run_adapter.py referenced at run_tools.py line 167 depends on that same layout), so relocating any file or adopting a real package install breaks it per-file with a bare ModuleNotFoundError. findings.title: Large embedded CSS and JS in html_report.py
findings.description: html_report.py embeds CSS (~113 lines, lines 8-120) and JavaScript (~48 lines, lines 122-169) as module-level string constants. These should ideally be in separate files or generated by a template engine. The embedding makes the Python code harder to edit and prevents syntax highlighting/linting of CSS/JS.
findings.impact: Reduces maintainability and developer experience. CSS and JS cannot be linted or syntax-highlighted when embedded in Python strings.
findings.remediation: Extract CSS to style.css and JS to script.js, or use a template engine. If embedding is necessary, add length comments marking sections.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The factual core of the claim is exact and verifiable. In /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/html_report.py, `_CSS = """` opens at line 8 and closes at line 120 (113 lines including delimiters, ~111 lines of CSS), and `_JS = """` spans lines 122-169 (48 lines). Both are module-level string constants, interpolated verbatim by `_html_doc()` at line 185 (`<style>{_CSS}</style>`) and line 191 (`<script>{_JS}</script>`). No separate .css/.js assets exist anywhere in the repo, so the CSS/JS genuinely receive no linting or syntax highlighting, and the module's first 169 lines are non-Python content. That much is CERTAIN. Confidence is only POSSIBLE for the finding as a whole because the normative half of the claim is contradicted by documented design intent: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-01-html-report-design.md:11-12 and :104 mandate 'Vanilla HTML/CSS/JS only - no frameworks, no CDNs, no external dependencies' and 'Self-contained artifact - one .html file with all CSS and JS inlined', and docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-html-report.md:7 specifies a 'stdlib-only module'. The claim's primary remediation is therefore partly unavailable: a template engine would add a third-party dependency the project explicitly forbids, and shipping style.css/script.js as external assets would break the single-file output contract asserted by the design spec. A source-side split that is read at render time and still inlined would preserve the contract, but it introduces __file__-relative path resolution into a skill that is distributed as a copied directory (tests reach it via sys.path.insert at tests/test_html_report.py:6), which is a real packaging tradeoff the current design deliberately avoids. The only remediation element that is unambiguously actionable and cost-free is the fallback suggestion to add section-marker comments. Severity LOW (arguably INFO) is appropriate; this is a documented tradeoff, not a defect. Separately, the attached citation CWE-1104 ('Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components') is inapplicable to embedded stylesheet/script constants and should not stand; it is already flagged verified:false with citation_quality 'minimal'. CWE-710 (Improper Adherence to Coding Standards) is the closest defensible mapping, and even it is weak. The cited path 'skill/scripts/html_report.py' is correct relative to the repo root.

findings.title: Helper name _depth_gte computes the inverse relation of what its name promises
findings.description: `_depth_gte(lens_depth, panel_depth)` reads as "lens_depth >= panel_depth" but its body returns `DEPTH_RANK.get(lens_depth, 0) <= DEPTH_RANK.get(panel_depth, 0)` — a <= comparison of the two ranks in that argument order. The call site (`plan_lenses`, `if not _depth_gte(threshold, depth): continue`) relies on this inverted meaning to implement the documented rule "lens.depth_threshold <= profile.depth", so the code is functionally correct today, but the identifier actively misleads about the comparison direction.
findings.impact: A maintainer reading or reusing this helper elsewhere is likely to assume it means "first arg is at least as deep as second arg" and pass arguments in the wrong order, silently breaking lens-spawn depth gating.
findings.remediation: Rename to something that matches the body's actual semantics, e.g. `_threshold_met(threshold_depth, actual_depth)`, or invert the body to match `_gte` and swap the call-site argument order; add a one-line docstring stating the comparison direction explicitly.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly against the source. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/depth_planner.py lines 8-9 read exactly: `def _depth_gte(lens_depth, panel_depth):` / `return DEPTH_RANK.get(lens_depth, 0) <= DEPTH_RANK.get(panel_depth, 0)`. With DEPTH_RANK = {shallow:0, standard:1, deep:2} (line 4), the body computes `rank(first arg) <= rank(second arg)`, i.e. 'first arg is at most as deep as second arg' — the strict inverse of what the `_gte` suffix promises for that argument order. There is no docstring or comment stating the intended direction. The single call site is line 32, `if not _depth_gte(threshold, depth): continue`, inside plan_lenses, whose docstring (line 18) documents the rule as `lens.depth_threshold <= profile.depth`; passing (threshold, depth) into a `<=` body implements that rule correctly, so the claim's assertion that the code is functionally correct today also holds. Behavior is locked in by /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_depth_planner.py (e.g. test_shallow_spawns_zero_or_one expects only the shallow-threshold lens under a shallow profile; test_deep_spawns_up_to_three expects deep-threshold lenses only under a deep profile), which is consistent with the <= semantics. Grep across the repo shows the helper has exactly one production call site and no other importers (only doc/plan copies at docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-multi-model-reviewer-dispatch.md:585-609 reproduce the same inverted naming, so the defect is also propagated into the design doc). The only mitigating nuance, which does not defeat the claim: the helper is module-private with a single caller and test coverage, so the 'silently breaking' impact is latent rather than active — appropriate for the LOW severity assigned. The claim's title, description, location, function name, and remediation all match the code verbatim. Note on citations: CWE-1099 (Inconsistent Naming Conventions for Identifiers) is a real CWE under the bad-coding-practices view and is a reasonable, if approximate, taxonomy match for a misleading identifier; it carries no direct security impact, consistent with the style category.

findings.title: Unescaped f-string interpolation of fixture paths into sh -c in check_fixtures()
findings.description: `check_fixtures()` builds a POSIX shell script by directly interpolating each fixture's `path` value (sourced from tests/fixtures/manifest.json) into a double-quoted `[ -d "{p}" ]` test with an f-string (line 54), joins them with `;`, and passes the resulting string to `docker run --rm <tag> sh -c <script>` with no shlex.quote/escaping. Any path value containing a shell metacharacter (quote, backtick, $(), ;) breaks out of the quoted context and executes as a shell command inside the fixtures container.
findings.impact: Under current usage the paths originate from the repo-local, version-controlled manifest.json, so exploitation requires an attacker able to modify that file (e.g. a malicious PR), and this docker invocation is --rm with no volume mounts, limiting blast radius to the throwaway panopticon-fixtures image. It remains a live CWE-78 injection primitive that becomes exploitable the moment manifest.json's provenance is less trusted or this pattern is reused with externally influenced paths.
findings.remediation: Avoid building a shell string: check each path with a separate no-shell `docker run --rm tag test -d "<path>"` invocation, or at minimum wrap each interpolated path in shlex.quote() before joining into the sh -c script.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The mechanical claim verifies verbatim. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py line 52 builds `cmd = ["docker", "run", "--rm", tag, "sh", "-c"]`; lines 53-56 build `test_script` by f-string interpolating each manifest `path` into `if [ -d "{p}" ]; then echo "PRESENT:{p}"; else echo "MISSING:{p}"; fi` and joining with `"; "`; line 57 appends it as the `sh -c` argument and line 58 executes it. No escaping is applied: grep for `shlex` across the whole skill/ tree returns zero hits (only reference/security-checklists.md mentions shell=True as a checklist item), so shlex is never imported anywhere in the codebase. A path containing `"`, a backtick, or `$(...)` therefore executes attacker-chosen commands inside the container. One precision defect in the claim: inside the double-quoted context a bare `;` (listed in the description's metacharacter set) does NOT break out, and backtick/`$()` execute via command substitution rather than by breaking quoting; the enumerated trigger set is looser than reality, but the underlying execution primitive is real. Trust-boundary analysis supports the claim's own self-limiting impact statement rather than contradicting it. MANIFEST is a module constant derived from `Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent.parent / "tests" / "fixtures" / "manifest.json"`, so it always resolves to panopticon's own repo tree and never to a scan target; grep across all .py files shows the manifest is only ever read (load_manifest, line 96) and never written by any code path; all four committed path values in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/fixtures/manifest.json are static `/opt/panopticon-fixtures/*` constants with no metacharacters. The CLI surface (--tag/--rebuild/--test) reaches docker only through list argv with no shell, so it adds no injection path. Reachability is weaker than the claim's "e.g. a malicious PR" implies: grep of /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/.github/workflows/ shows this harness is never invoked in CI (the only fixture reference in security.yml is an exclude_globs entry), and it is documented purely as a manual developer command in skill/SKILL.md lines 104-110 and DEVELOPMENT.md lines 78-81 — so exploitation additionally requires a maintainer to check out the untrusted branch and run the harness locally. Blast radius is as described: that docker run has no -v mounts, no docker socket, no --privileged, and uses --rm, so injected commands are confined to the throwaway panopticon-fixtures image (the separate run_tests() invocation does mount repo paths, but read-only and with no shell interpolation). Note that an earlier scan record in /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-self-scan-report.json (discarded_claims, CMD-078) rejected this same pattern, but explicitly on severity grounds — "a shlex.quote hardening nit, not HIGH" — which concedes the pattern is genuine. SEC-203 is filed at LOW/POSSIBLE and already discloses the trusted-source precondition and the contained blast radius, so it is consistent with that prior reasoning rather than a re-litigation of it. Confidence is LIKELY rather than CERTAIN because the code facts are certain but the finding is a latent hardening issue with no currently crossable trust boundary, and the remediation (per-path `docker run --rm tag test -d <path>` argv, or shlex.quote before joining) is sound and directly implementable given docker is already invoked with list argv.

findings.title: Self-asserted _group field can misattribute a finding to the wrong review group when the source filename doesn't match GROUP_RE
findings.description: `load_findings()` derives a finding's internal `_group` tag from the source filename via `GROUP_RE` (lines 119-120) and only overwrites `nf["_group"]` when that match succeeds. `normalize_finding()` mutates the finding dict in place and returns the same object, so if the incoming agent JSON already carries a `_group` key — an internal-only field never documented in the panel-review/lens-sweep finding schema — and the filename fails to match GROUP_RE (e.g. an unusual group name, or any file not produced through the standard dispatch out_file convention), the self-asserted value passes through untouched into build_report()'s per-group bucketing (lines 636-653), which decides which group's panel_grades/key_findings the finding is counted under, before being stripped from the final report at line 657.
findings.impact: A compromised or prompt-injected reviewer for one group could relabel one of its own findings into a different group's bucket, hiding it from the correct group's per-group grade/key_findings while it surfaces under an unrelated group. Global summary.stats/gate are unaffected, so this is a per-group reporting-integrity gap rather than a gate bypass, but can still mislead any consumer that gates or triages by per-group grade.
findings.remediation: Strip any pre-existing _group key from agent-authored JSON in load_findings() (fold it into the same denylist as SEC-201) before assigning the filename-derived value, rather than only conditionally overwriting it.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified the mechanism end to end in the code. (1) /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/synthesize.py:119-133 matches the claim verbatim: `m = GROUP_RE.match(os.path.basename(path))`, `group = m.group(1) if m else None`, then the AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS denylist (line 93: only `source` and `reinforced`) is applied, and `nf["_group"] = group` executes only `if group is not None`. `normalize_finding()` (lines 47-85) mutates and returns the same dict and never strips unknown/underscore keys, so an agent-authored `_group` survives untouched whenever GROUP_RE fails. (2) The tainted value is load-bearing: build_report at lines 636-643 buckets per group with `(f.get("_group") == g["name"]) or (f.get("_group") not in known_groups and location.file in gfiles)`. Asserting a _known_ group name both pulls the finding into that group's `panel_grades`/`key_findings` (lines 646-652) and suppresses the file-membership fallback for its true group, so the finding disappears from the correct group's per-group grade/key_findings. `_group` is popped at line 657 before emission, and evidence.py:129-130 strips underscore keys from the verify queue, so it never appears in artifacts — matching the claim's 'stripped from the final report' detail. (3) Blast radius as claimed: `summary.stats`, `overall_grade`, `risk_level` and `gate` derive from `active`/`gate_eligible`/`by_panel` (lines 626-634, 655, 669-679), none of which consult `_group`. So this is per-group reporting integrity, not a gate bypass — LOW is the right severity. (4) `_group` is genuinely internal-only: skill/agents/panel-review.md's 'Finding format' (lines 31-63) never documents it, and the only legitimate writers are ingest_tools' adapters (scripts/tools/*.py) whose findings enter via ingest_tools.ingest_dir at synthesize.py:919-922, bypassing load_findings entirely — so the proposed denylist fix would not regress tool findings. (5) Reachability requires the conjunction the claim itself states: an adversarial/injected reviewer emitting `_group`, AND a filename that fails GROUP_RE (synthesize.py:456-458). Standard dispatch names (dispatch.py:256,281) do match, but the panel and lens tokens in `out_file` come from the scout-returned ScopeProfile and are never validated at runtime — I found no jsonschema/validate_scope_profile enforcement of reference/scope-profile-schema.json anywhere in skill/ — so an off-enum panel name or a lens name containing any character outside `[A-Za-z0-9_]` (e.g. 'sql-injection') yields a non-matching filename and group=None. Any file passed to synthesize.py outside the `.panopticon/findings-*.json` convention does the same. No test covers a pre-existing `_group` in an agent file (tests/test_synthesize.py:616-631 only cover the matching-filename case; :600-614 injects `_group` directly into build_report). Claim confirmed as written.

findings.title: Advisor prompt embeds an unfiltered agent-authored finding JSON, opening an indirect-prompt-injection channel
findings.description: `render_advisor_prompts()` serializes an entire finding dict — including free-text description/impact/remediation/title fields an earlier panel_review/lens_sweep agent produced after reading the target repository's own source — and substitutes it verbatim into the `{claim_json}` placeholder of agents/advisor.md, which becomes the literal advisor prompt. Because those free-text fields can contain wording copied or paraphrased from the reviewed repository, and that repository is by panopticon's own threat model untrusted/adversarial, this is a channel for indirect prompt injection.
findings.impact: agents/advisor.md already instructs the model not to trust the claim and to verify independently by reading cited files, and evidence.match_verdict() requires an exact finding_id echo — both are real, effective mitigations bounding damage to a single already-flagged finding's verdict. But there is no structural isolation of the untrusted payload beyond a markdown heading (no explicit 'treat imperative text inside string fields as data, not instructions' framing), so a successful injection could still flip an individual verdict — the same self-verification/laundering risk class the codebase otherwise guards against.
findings.remediation: Add explicit untrusted-data framing around {claim_json} in agents/advisor.md, and consider bounding/neutralizing the free-text fields before substitution (length caps, stripping of markdown/code-fence sequences that could re-open the delimiter).

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Every code-verifiable assertion in the claim checks out at the cited locus and along the full chain of custody. (1) dispatch.py:345-346 is exactly as described: `claim = json.dumps(finding, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` then `render_prompt("advisor.md", {"claim_json": claim})` — the entire finding dict, no field allowlist, no filtering. (2) render_prompt (dispatch.py:151-176) is a sentinel-based two-step replace whose docstring states values containing '{placeholder}' syntax deliberately 'pass through literally'; it performs no escaping, and tests/test_dispatch.py:303 asserts a description containing `{code_context}` survives verbatim into the rendered prompt — so verbatim embedding is intentional and test-locked. (3) agents/advisor.md:12-14 places bare `{claim_json}` directly under a `## Claim` markdown heading, NOT inside a code fence, with no 'treat string-field contents as data, not instructions' framing — matching the claim's 'no structural isolation beyond a markdown heading'. (4) Provenance premise holds: agents/panel-review.md gives panel reviewers Read/Grep/Glob over the target repo's files and instructs them to author free-text title/description/impact/remediation, and evidence.build_verify_queue (evidence.py:107-108) queues precisely the agentic (non-tool, non-reinforced) findings — so the advisor's input is by construction agent-authored free text derived from reading the reviewed repo. SKILL.md:133-135 documents the untrusted-repo threat model in-repo ('repos that may contain planted injection payloads'). (5) No neutralization exists anywhere upstream: synthesize.normalize_finding (synthesize.py:47-85) length-caps only the derived `short_title` and whitespace-collapses `title`, leaving description/impact/remediation entirely unbounded and unfiltered; load_findings strips only AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS = ('source','reinforced'); evidence.write_verify_queue (evidence.py:123-136) strips only '_'-prefixed keys; render_advisor_prompts validates only entry shape and the queue_id path-safety regex. Notably the codebase already recognizes agent payloads as untrusted for trust-conferring fields (AGENT_FORBIDDEN_FIELDS, per its own SEC-102), which makes the absence of free-text framing a consistent gap rather than a design decision. (6) The mitigations the claim credits are real and correctly characterized: advisor.md:9-10 ('Do not trust the claim; verify it') and evidence.match_verdict (evidence.py:202-221), which drops any verdict whose finding_id echo mismatches; evidence.apply_verdict (evidence.py:224-238) never touches severity or confidence. Damage is therefore bounded to one already-flagged finding, but is not nil: confirmation_status feeds evidence status, and per SKILL.md:121-127 a flipped verdict moves a real finding to discarded_claims or makes a bogus one advisor_confirmed and thus CI-gate-eligible, plus apply_verdict merges attacker-influenced reasoning/citations/references into the report. This very prompt file (.panopticon/advisor-prompts/039-SEC-204.md, lines 6-48) is a rendered instance and empirically demonstrates the unfenced raw-JSON embedding. findings.title: Self-contained HTML report ships an inline <script> with no Content-Security-Policy
findings.description: `_html_doc()` emits a <style> block and an inline <script>{_JS}</script> but no Content-Security-Policy meta tag. Every dynamic field reaching the document today is correctly passed through _escape() (html.escape, quote=True) before interpolation (verified across _render_card, _render_provenance, _render_heatmap, etc.), so there is no live XSS, but the document has no defense-in-depth against a future regression, and the report renders agent- and tool-authored strings that ultimately reflect content from the potentially adversarial reviewed repository.
findings.impact: Low today — no injection point exists — but a future escaping regression in the finding-rendering helpers would fail open (execute) rather than fail closed, and if the report is ever hosted over HTTP without an external CSP header this is the only layer available.
findings.remediation: Add a restrictive CSP meta tag in _html_doc(), or better, hash/nonce the inline _JS/_CSS blocks and drop 'unsafe-inline' for script-src so an escaping regression is contained.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. `_html_doc()` at skill/scripts/html_report.py:177-193 emits exactly two meta tags (`charset` and `viewport`), an inline `` at line 185 and an inline `` at line 191. The output is a standalone file written by `write_html()` (line 676) with no HTTP layer, so no external CSP header can exist either. The factual core of the claim — inline script, no CSP, INFO/defense-in-depth severity — is exactly right, and CWE-693 (Protection Mechanism Failure) plus A05:2021 are the correct classifications for a missing defense-in-depth control. One correction to the claim's supporting rationale, which makes the finding stronger rather than weaker: the description asserts that *every* dynamic field is passed through `_escape()`. That is not quite true. `_render_citation_quality()` at line 327 interpolates the value raw into a single-quoted class attribute: `f"{_escape(quality)}"` — the text node is escaped but the attribute token is not. This is the same bug class that was already fixed once next door in `_render_provenance()` (lines 313-315 carry a `SEC-101` comment and apply `re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9-]", "-", ...)` to the status token); `_render_citation_quality` was missed by that fix. In the normal synthesize pipeline the value is not attacker-controlled: `citations.enrich_citations()` overwrites `citation_quality` on every finding with the fixed vocabulary returned by `_compute_citation_quality()` (citations.py:184-202 -> only "full"/"partial"/"minimal"/"none"), `evidence.derive_evidence()` copies that into `evidence.citation_quality`, and synthesize.py:624 pops the top-level key. However, the `--compare` path at synthesize.py:861-887 `json.load()`s two report files straight off disk and passes them to `html_report.write_html()` with no schema validation, no `enrich_citations()` and no `derive_evidence()`, so `evidence.citation_quality` is rendered verbatim from whatever JSON was supplied. A value such as `partial' onmouseover='...` would break out of that attribute. So a live (if narrow, non-default, INFO-grade) attribute-injection sink already exists and is reachable — precisely the fail-open regression the claim predicts, which is the argument for the CSP the claim asks for. All other interpolations I checked are safe: `_severity_class`/`_panel_class` strip to alphanumerics (lines 292-306), `_gate_class` maps to a fixed set, the bar-chart width is `{pct:.1f}` numeric, tab tokens come from the fixed `_SEV_ORDER`, the delta badge is escaped and drawn from the internal `_match_findings` vocabulary, and reference hrefs are `_escape`d with `html.escape` default `quote=True` and gated on an `http(s)://` prefix. CONFIRMED as an INFO defense-in-depth finding. The recommended remediation (restrictive CSP meta tag, ideally hash/nonce the inline blocks and drop 'unsafe-inline' for script-src) is sound; it should be paired with sanitizing the `cit-{quality}` class token the same way `prov-{status_class}` was.

findings.title: Untested fixture test orchestration logic
findings.description: run_fixture_tests.py has no unit tests. The main() function (lines 102-138) orchestrates Docker image building, fixture validation, and pytest execution. Complex conditional logic (lines 119-132) handles image existence, rebuild requirements, and fixture presence checks with no test coverage.
findings.impact: Docker integration issues, fixture validation failures, and test execution problems may not be detected until CI runtime, increasing time-to-feedback.
findings.remediation: Add unit tests (with mocked Docker calls) covering image existence checks, build_image() invocation, check_fixtures() with present/missing fixtures, and run_tests() with various exit codes.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py exists and matches the cited structure: main() spans lines 102-138 (the location's line_end 142 merely extends through the `if __name__ == '__main__'` block at 141-142), and the conditional orchestration the claim describes is at lines 119-132 (`if args.rebuild or not image_exists(args.tag): build_image(...) else: print('Using existing image')`, then check_fixtures() at 125, then run_tests() at 132). A grep of the entire tests/ tree for `run_fixture_tests|build_image|check_fixtures|run_tests|docker_available|image_exists` returns only four hits, all in tests/test_run_tools.py and all against `scripts.run_tools.docker_available` (a different module, imported at test_run_tools.py:4 as `import scripts.run_tools as rt`). No test file imports or exercises run_fixture_tests.py. This is a deviation from the repo's own convention: every other module in skill/scripts (citations, depth_planner, orchestrator, provenance, model_resolver, ingest_tools, run_tools, dispatch, evidence, html_report, synthesize) has a matching tests/test_<module>.py; run_fixture_tests.py is the only user-facing script with none. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs only `python -m pytest tests/ -q` plus ruff, never invokes the script, and no coverage tooling or config exists (pyproject.toml has only ruff config), so the gap is invisible to the pipeline; DEVELOPMENT.md:79-80 documents the script as a manually-invoked developer entry point. The claim's impact is not hypothetical: the untested code contains at least two concrete latent defects that mocked-subprocess unit tests would catch. (1) docker_available() at lines 22-27 calls subprocess.run(['docker','version']) with no FileNotFoundError guard, so on a host without the docker binary it raises an uncaught traceback instead of reaching the intended `print('error: docker is not available or not running'); return 1` at main() lines 109-111 — notably, the sibling run_tools.docker_available() takes an injectable `runner` and IS tested for exactly this case (test_run_tools.py:9-12), showing the untested copy diverged. (2) check_fixtures() at line 58 discards result.returncode entirely; if `docker run` fails, stdout is empty, both `present` and `missing_paths` stay empty, and main() prints a Summary of 'Fixtures present: 0 / Fixtures missing: 0' with no error signal — a silent-success failure mode. Two calibration caveats for the auditor, neither of which contradicts the finding: severity HIGH looks inflated for a developer-only test harness with no runtime, network, or security exposure (MEDIUM/LOW fits the maintainability impact better), and the CWE-391 citation is a poor fit for 'missing unit tests' as a class — though it happens to describe defect (2) above accurately, so I cite it against that specific line rather than against the coverage gap itself.

findings.title: Citation enrichment exception handling not directly tested
findings.description: The enrich_citations() function (lines 219-280) contains a broad exception handler at line 266 that catches all exceptions during citation enrichment. This is intentionally tolerant to prevent synthesis failures, but the exception path (lines 266-269) lacks explicit test coverage for the graceful degradation behavior when enrichment fails.
findings.impact: Silent failures in citation enrichment could result in findings without CWE/OWASP mappings. Debugging citation issues becomes difficult without test validation of error handling.
findings.remediation: Add test cases in test_citations.py for enrich_citations() covering malformed citation data causing exception, that findings still serialize correctly, and that citation_quality is set to 'none' on error.
references: skill/scripts/citations.py:60 (validate_cwe catalog["cwe"] — the reachable KeyError trigger)
skill/scripts/citations.py:208,240,245,250-251 (isinstance guards that absorb all malformed-data inputs)
tests/test_citations.py:308-318 (test_enrich_tolerant_of_malformed_subfields — exercises tolerant happy path, not the handler)
tests/test_citations.py:18-29 (test_missing_catalog_degrades_gracefully — normalized empty catalog, still no exception)
skill/scripts/synthesize.py:620,924 (callers, both pass a well-formed catalog)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified directly against the code and the full test suite. (1) Location is accurate: /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/citations.py defines enrich_citations at line 219 and the function body ends at line 281; line 266 is `except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - citation enrichment must never abort synthesis`, and the handler body (267-269) prints to stderr, does `f.pop("citations", None)`, and sets `f["citation_quality"] = "none"`. (2) The test file the claim names does exist (at repo-root tests/, not skill/): /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_citations.py, and enrich_citations is well covered there (18 call sites; no other test file in the repo calls it directly). (3) The gap is real: I traced every one of those call sites and none can reach lines 267-269. The closest candidate, test_enrich_tolerant_of_malformed_subfields (test_citations.py:308-318), feeds ssvc-as-string, cwe-as-int and cve/owasp-as-int, but every one of those is absorbed by upstream isinstance guards inside the try (`_raw_cwe_ids` returns [] for a non-list at citations.py:208; `owasp_raw if isinstance(owasp_raw, list) else []` at line 240; `inputs = inputs if isinstance(inputs, dict) else {}` at line 245; the CVE list comprehension at 250-251). Those findings exit through the normal path at 261-265, not the handler — the test's own comment ('must not raise') confirms it asserts the try body succeeds. Likewise test_missing_catalog_degrades_gracefully (test_citations.py:18-29) passes the *normalized* empty catalog from load_cwe_catalog, which always returns all three keys ('cwe', 'cwe_owasp', 'owasp_top10' — citations.py:48-52), so `catalog["cwe"]` in validate_cwe never raises; that test also explicitly asserts enrichment runs 'without raising'. Note also that a non-dict finding is NOT protected: `raw = f.get("citations")` at line 223 sits outside the try and would raise AttributeError uncaught — a separate untested path. (5) Two accuracy caveats on the claim's framing, neither of which defeats it: the failure is not fully 'silent' (it logs to stderr at line 267), and citation_quality='none' does not drop the finding — it flows into evidence.derive_evidence (skill/scripts/evidence.py:42-71) as metadata and is then popped from the finding (synthesize.py:624), so the real impact is degraded CWE/OWASP metadata and quality scoring, not data loss. findings.title: test_synthesize.py calls unittest.mock.patch without importing unittest.mock
findings.description: TestHtmlOut.test_compare_missing_file_errors_cleanly (line 1027) and test_compare_invalid_json_errors_cleanly (line 1050) reference `unittest.mock.patch(...)`, but the file only does `import unittest` at the top (line 7) — there is no `import unittest.mock` or `from unittest import mock` anywhere in tests/test_synthesize.py. `unittest.mock` is a separate submodule that Python does not auto-attach to the `unittest` package on `import unittest`; the attribute only exists once something in the process has explicitly imported `unittest.mock`. Every sibling test file that uses mock.patch (test_dispatch.py, test_model_resolver.py) imports it explicitly via `from unittest import mock`; this file is the odd one out.
findings.impact: The two tests pass today only because some other import in the same process has already attached `mock` to the `unittest` module object by the time they run. That is an accidental, unstated dependency on test collection/import order. Running this file in isolation with a runner that does not pre-load unittest.mock raises `AttributeError: module 'unittest' has no attribute 'mock'` instead of exercising the intended stderr-capture assertions.
findings.remediation: Add `from unittest import mock` to the top-level imports of tests/test_synthesize.py and reference it as `mock.patch(...)`, matching test_dispatch.py and test_model_resolver.py.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Verified directly from source. tests/test_synthesize.py's only unittest-related import is `import unittest` at line 7; a grep for `unittest.mock|from unittest import mock|import mock` across the whole file returns zero import statements and exactly two usages: line 1027 (`with unittest.mock.patch("sys.stderr", new_callable=io.StringIO) as captured:` inside test_compare_missing_file_errors_cleanly, which begins at line 1011) and line 1050 (same call inside test_compare_invalid_json_errors_cleanly, beginning at line 1032). Both are members of class TestHtmlOut (declared at line 967), so the claim's location span 1027-1050 is accurate; the only imprecision is that the claim labels 1027/1050 as the function start lines rather than the patch-call lines, which does not affect the substance.

`unittest.mock` is a submodule, not an attribute bound by `import unittest`. CPython's unittest/__init__.py imports .result/.case/.suite/.loader/.main/.runner/.signals and exposes a module-level __getattr__ that lazily resolves only IsolatedAsyncioTestCase; it never imports .mock. The attribute `unittest.mock` therefore exists only after some code in the process explicitly imports unittest.mock, which binds it onto the parent package.

I confirmed nothing in the file's own import graph supplies it. The module under test, skill/scripts/synthesize.py, imports only argparse, hashlib, glob, json, os, re, sys plus scripts.citations, scripts.evidence, scripts.html_report, scripts.ingest_tools; a grep for `unittest` across all of skill/scripts returns a single hit that is a comment in scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py line 22. There is no conftest.py anywhere in the repo and no tests/__init__.py, so no collection-time hook pre-imports mock either.

The accidental-pass mechanism the claim describes is real and I traced it. CI runs the whole directory in one process (.github/workflows/ci.yml line 41: `python -m pytest tests/ -q`), and pytest completes collection (importing every test module) before executing tests. Sibling modules that do import it include tests/test_dispatch.py line 8 (`from unittest import mock`), tests/test_model_resolver.py line 7 (`from unittest.mock import patch`), and ten files under tests/tools/. Any one of those binds `mock` onto the unittest package object, so the two tests pass in a full-suite run purely as a side effect of import order.

The isolated-run failure mode is reachable in this repo's documented workflow, not hypothetical: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-html-report.md prescribes `pytest tests/test_synthesize.py::TestHtmlOut -v` at lines 927 and 997 — exactly the class holding both affected tests. In that invocation nothing imports unittest.mock (pytest deliberately avoids importing it; its num_mock_patch_args helper probes `sys.modules.get("unittest.mock")` rather than importing), so both tests would raise AttributeError: module 'unittest' has no attribute 'mock' before reaching the intended stderr assertions. The one point I could not settle statically is whether some pytest plugin present in a given environment happens to import unittest.mock; that only affects whether the latent breakage is observed today, not whether the missing import exists. I therefore mark the defect CERTAIN.

Severity MEDIUM is defensible: this is a latent, order-dependent test that silently degrades from an assertion to an error, and the remediation (add `from unittest import mock` and call `mock.patch(...)`, matching tests/test_dispatch.py) is exact and correct. CWE-710 (Improper Adherence to Coding Standards) is an appropriate, if generic, mapping.

findings.title: run_fixture_tests.py has no unit tests and no injectable subprocess seam
findings.description: There is no tests/test_run_fixture_tests.py anywhere in the repo, so `load_manifest`, `check_fixtures`, `image_exists`, `docker_available`, `build_image`, `run_tests`, and `main`'s argument handling have zero automated test coverage. This is unlike the closely related skill/scripts/run_tools.py, which was explicitly refactored to accept an injectable `runner` parameter precisely so its docker-invoking logic could be unit tested with fakes (see tests/test_run_tools.py). run_fixture_tests.py instead calls `subprocess.run` directly and unconditionally in docker_available, image_exists, build_image, and run_tests (lines 17-19, 23-27, 31-35, 38-44, 79-88), with no parameter to substitute a fake process.
findings.impact: Pure, easily-testable logic — manifest JSON parsing/validation, the PRESENT:/MISSING: stdout-parsing in check_fixtures, and the pytest-args construction in run_tests — can regress silently, since the only way this code is exercised is by actually building the panopticon-fixtures Docker image, a manual/CI-gated integration path not part of `pytest tests/ -q`.
findings.remediation: Add tests/test_run_fixture_tests.py covering load_manifest and check_fixtures's stdout-parsing, and give docker_available/image_exists/build_image/run_tests an injectable runner parameter mirroring run_tools.py's pattern.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
Every factual assertion in the claim is directly verifiable and holds.

(1) No test file exists. A repo-wide glob for `**/test_*.py` returns 40 files, none named `test_run_fixture_tests.py`. A repo-wide grep for `run_fixture_tests` matches only DEVELOPMENT.md (docs), Dockerfile.fixtures:56 (`CMD ["python", "skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py"]`), SKILL.md, and prior self-scan report JSON — never a test. A grep for `run_fixture_tests|fixture_tests` scoped to `tests/` returns no matches at all, so the module is never imported, monkeypatched, or otherwise exercised by the suite. A glob for `**/*test*.py` under `skill/` returns only `scripts/run_fixture_tests.py` itself, confirming there is no co-located test directory. `tests/test_dockerfile.py` also does not reference it.

(2) The subprocess calls are direct and unconditional, at the cited lines. Reading the file confirms: `run()` helper at 17-19 calls `subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, **kwargs)`; `docker_available()` at 22-27 calls `subprocess.run(["docker", "version"], capture_output=True)`; `image_exists()` at 30-35 calls `subprocess.run(["docker", "image", "inspect", tag], ...)`; `build_image()` at 38-44 calls the module-level `run()`; `run_tests()` at 79-88 builds the docker argv and calls `subprocess.run(cmd)`. None of these takes a runner/injection parameter. The claim understates the problem slightly in its favor: `check_fixtures()` also calls `subprocess.run` directly at line 58, and `load_manifest()` reads the hardcoded module-level `MANIFEST` constant (line 13), so it too has no seam.

(3) The contrast with run_tools.py is accurate, not rhetorical. Grepping `skill/scripts/run_tools.py` for `runner` shows `docker_available(image="panopticon-tools", runner=None)` at line 36, `run_adapters(..., runner=None)` at 94, and `run_tools(..., runner=None)` at 115, each with the `runner = runner or subprocess.run` default. `tests/test_run_tools.py` imports `scripts.run_tools as rt` and exploits exactly that seam with fake runners in at least a dozen tests (e.g. `rt.docker_available(runner=runner)`, `rt.run_tools(d, ["semgrep"], out_dir, runner=runner)`), including one that asserts the exact docker argv. So the sibling script was demonstrably refactored for testability and this one was not.

(4) The impact claim about CI holds. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` line 41 runs `python -m pytest tests/ -q` as the sole test step; there is no job that builds `panopticon-fixtures` or invokes `run_fixture_tests.py`. `pyproject.toml` defines no pytest config that would widen collection. Therefore the manifest JSON parsing/validation, the `PRESENT:`/`MISSING:` stdout parsing in `check_fixtures` (lines 61-68), and the pytest-args construction in `run_tests` (lines 74-78) are reachable only by a human running the script against a real Docker daemon, and can regress without any CI signal.

The finding is a genuine test-design gap rather than an exploitable security vulnerability, so MEDIUM severity and the generic CWE-710 mapping are defensible but the CWE is a weak fit; no OWASP or CVE mapping is warranted.

findings.title: citations.normalize_cwe_entries is unused in production code and untested
findings.description: `normalize_cwe_entries` (citations.py:66-80) is exported from the module but is not called anywhere in citations.py's own pipeline — `enrich_citations` builds its CWE list via `_raw_cwe_ids` + `validate_cwe` directly (lines 232-235) rather than through this helper — nor is it called from any other file under skill/. Grepping the whole test tree turns up zero references to the function.
findings.impact: This is either genuinely dead code (unnecessary maintenance surface) or a helper that some caller was meant to use and doesn't (a latent integration gap). Either way it sits with no regression protection: the documented behavior could silently break and nothing would notice.
findings.remediation: Either delete normalize_cwe_entries if confirmed unused, or wire it into its intended call site and add unit tests for its three documented behaviors.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Verified independently. (1) The definition is exactly where the claim says: `def normalize_cwe_entries(entries, catalog, tool_sourced=False)` at citations.py:66, body ending `return out` at line 80. (2) A repo-wide grep for `normalize_cwe_entries` (no type filter, hidden directories included -- .panopticon/ and .panopticon.prev-20260803/ both appeared in adjacent greps, so coverage is real) returns exactly one hit: the definition line itself. Zero call sites in production code, zero in the test tree. A looser grep for `normalize_cwe` returns 8 hits across 3 files, but the other 7 are a different, private, and separately tested helper -- `dependency_check._normalize_cwe` (scripts/tools/dependency_check.py:45, called at :65, covered by tests/tools/test_dependency_check.py:42-47). (3) The claim's specific assertion about the pipeline is accurate: enrich_citations builds its CWE list inline at citations.py:232-235 via `for cid in _raw_cwe_ids(raw): v = validate_cwe(cid, catalog, tool_sourced=tool_sourced)`, bypassing the helper entirely. (4) No test coverage: tests/test_citations.py does a plain `import citations as cit` (line 8, no wildcard import that could hide indirect use) and its ~45 test methods cover load_cwe_catalog, validate_cwe, derive_owasp, ssvc_decide, epss_lookup, _compute_citation_quality and enrich_citations -- none touch normalize_cwe_entries. (5) The only importer of the module, synthesize.py (`import scripts.citations as citations`, line 14), references only `citations.load_cwe_catalog` and `citations.enrich_citations` (lines 620, 923-924). No getattr-based or dynamic dispatch onto the module exists. Two minor imprecisions in the claim that do not change the verdict: citations.py defines no `__all__` (only ingest_tools.py:26 does), so "exported" means only that the name is public/top-level; and the claim's hedge that this may be "a helper some caller was meant to use" is the weaker reading -- the evidence favors plain dead code, because enrich_citations supersedes it and is strictly stricter. discarded_claims.title: Global mutable singleton state without thread safety
discarded_claims.description: The module uses a module-level global `_PROFILES` variable (line 35) with a singleton pattern via `_profiles()` (lines 38-42). This introduces implicit global state that is not thread-safe and makes concurrent invocations problematic.
discarded_claims.impact: Concurrent calls to resolve_model() may experience race conditions when the global _PROFILES is being modified. Unit testing becomes difficult due to shared state between tests.
discarded_claims.remediation: Refactor to eliminate module-level mutable state. Consider dependency injection of profiles or lazy initialization within a thread-safe context manager.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The structural facts are accurate but the claimed impact is contradicted by the code. (1) Lines 35-42 do contain `_PROFILES = None` plus a lazy `_profiles()` memoizer, exactly as described. (2) However `_PROFILES` is write-once, never mutated after initialization: a repo-wide grep for `_PROFILES` across all *.py finds assignments only at model_resolver.py:35 and :41, plus two `patch.object` uses in tests. The impact statement 'race conditions when the global _PROFILES is being modified' describes mutation that does not exist. (3) The lazy-init pattern is race-benign even under threads: `_PROFILES` is rebound only after `_load_profiles()` has returned a fully constructed object, so no partially-initialized value is ever observable; module-global rebinding is atomic under CPython. The worst case for two racing threads is a redundant YAML read and a duplicate stderr warning, both idempotent — never an incorrect resolution. (4) The claimed concurrent path cannot execute in this repository: a repo-wide grep over all *.py for `import threading|from threading|concurrent.futures|ThreadPool|multiprocessing|asyncio` returns zero matches. The only non-test consumer is skill/scripts/dispatch.py (imports at line 11, calls at lines 261 and 286), a synchronous argparse CLI with an `if __name__ == "__main__"` entrypoint at line 441; panopticon parallelism is agent/subprocess-level, and each process gets its own interpreter and its own module state. (5) The 'unit testing becomes difficult' impact is directly falsified by tests/test_model_resolver.py:79 and :83, which override the cache via `with patch.object(mr, "_PROFILES", {})` and are auto-restored by unittest.mock; the surrounding tests exercise env/CLI/fallback precedence without state leakage. One adjacent, genuinely real but LOW-severity issue that the claim does not make: resolve_model() lines 119-121 return `cfg` by reference out of the cached profiles dict, so a caller that mutates the returned dict would corrupt the process-wide cache. dispatch.py does not mutate it (it embeds the dict into the plan and serializes with json.dump), so there is no live defect today. That aliasing nit does not support a HIGH-severity thread-safety finding.
