discarded_claims.title: Thread-unsafe global mutable state in model_resolver.py
discarded_claims.description: model_resolver.py uses a module-level global variable _PROFILES (line 35) that is mutated by the _profiles() function (lines 38-42) via lazy initialization. This pattern is not thread-safe: if multiple threads call _profiles() simultaneously, race conditions could occur leading to inconsistent state or multiple redundant loads.
discarded_claims.impact: In multi-threaded execution contexts, simultaneous calls to _profiles() could cause data races, memory inconsistency, or redundant expensive operations.
discarded_claims.remediation: Either protect access with threading.Lock, use functools.lru_cache for thread-safe caching, or initialize _PROFILES at import time. For CLI-only usage, document the single-threaded assumption.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning:
The code pattern is described accurately, but the claim is rejected on two independent grounds: the claimed execution path cannot occur, and the claimed impact is not achievable even hypothetically.

(1) Pattern is real. /Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/skill/scripts/model_resolver.py line 35 is `_PROFILES = None` and lines 38-42 are the lazy-init `def _profiles(): global _PROFILES; if _PROFILES is None: _PROFILES = _load_profiles(); return _PROFILES`. So the structural description is factually correct.

(2) No multi-threaded context exists. A repo-wide grep of all *.py for `threading|ThreadPool|concurrent.futures|multiprocessing|asyncio|Thread\(` returned ZERO matches. Glob confirms exactly one model_resolver.py. Grepping all *.py for importers shows only two consumers: skill/scripts/dispatch.py (line 11 `import model_resolver`, calling `resolve_model` at lines 261 and 286 inside a plain sequential `for panel_name in ...` loop) and tests/test_model_resolver.py. dispatch.py is a one-shot CLI with a `def main(argv=None)` at line 354 and an `if __name__ == "__main__"` guard at line 441, documented in skill/SKILL.md lines 46/56/80 as `python3 scripts/dispatch.py ...`. The 'parallel' language in SKILL.md (lines 20, 58, 75) refers to agent/subprocess-level fan-out via the Agent tool, not in-process threads — separate OS processes each get their own independent copy of module globals, so `_PROFILES` cannot be shared or raced across them.

(3) The impact is overstated even under a hypothetical threaded caller. `_load_profiles()` fully constructs the dict (yaml.safe_load, or `{}` on ImportError/OSError/YAMLError) and returns it before it is ever published; the `global` rebinding of a module attribute is a single atomic name binding under CPython, and remains atomic under free-threaded builds. The worst possible outcome is that N threads each redundantly read the same static, idempotent reference/model-profiles.yml and one assignment wins; every reader thereafter observes a fully-constructed, semantically equivalent dict. 'Data races, memory inconsistency' and 'inconsistent state' as stated in the impact field are not reachable outcomes for this idiom — the only true element is 'redundant loads' of a cheap local file read, which is a negligible performance note, not a defect.

(4) The citation is also mismapped: CWE-413 is 'Improper Resource Locking', which concerns locking of a shared resource; the idiom described would map to CWE-543 ('Use of Singleton Pattern Without Synchronization in a Multithreaded Context') if it were valid at all. The citation was already flagged verified:false.

Residual note for the auditor: nothing here would break if a future consumer imported model_resolver into a threaded host, but no such consumer exists today, and the failure mode would still be a redundant file read rather than corruption. This is at most a latent style/documentation preference, not a LOW-severity defect.

(2) The coupling is one-directional and acyclic. An entry point depending on the domain modules it orchestrates is correct layering, not a coupling defect; inverting it would be needless indirection.

(3) 'Inhibits independent evolution of subsystems' is empirically false. Modules that are independently importable and independently tested are by definition independently evolvable.

The actual call surface is narrow and passes only plain data (lists of finding dicts, the report dict): html_report is used via exactly one function (write_html, 2 call sites); ingest_tools via exactly one (ingest_dir, 1 call site); citations via two (load_cwe_catalog, enrich_citations). html_report.py exposes only two public functions total. Grepping for `(citations|evidence_mod|html_report|ingest_tools)\._[a-zA-Z]` returned no matches — synthesize never reaches into private internals, and there is no shared mutable module state.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's descriptive skeleton is accurate but trivial; its load-bearing impact rationale is contradicted by the code. (1) 'Template paths are hard-coded in multiple places' is false. TEMPLATE_DIR is defined exactly once (skill/scripts/dispatch.py:14) and is referenced only inside load_template (lines 72 and 74). Repo-wide grep confirms no other occurrence in dispatch.py. Every consumer funnels through that single loader: emit_host_agents calls load_template at line 117, render_prompt at line 162, and render_advisor_prompts reaches it via render_prompt('advisor.md', ...) at line 346. That is one choke point, the opposite of the claim. (2) 'Difficult to change template storage mechanism' is false: changing storage means editing one function. discarded_claims.title: Tuple size mismatch breaks deduplication logic in model collection
discarded_claims.description: The function collects unique (model, role) pairs into a set using 2-tuples as keys (line 188: key = (model, role)). However, when processing advisor confirmations, a 3-tuple is added (line 198: advisor_key = (confirmed_by_model, None, "advisor")). Since Python tuples of different lengths are never equal, the 3-tuple will never match existing 2-tuples in the set, breaking the deduplication logic entirely.
discarded_claims.impact: Duplicate advisor entries with the same model may be added to the output list, causing incorrect model/role reporting in CodeReviewReport metadata.
discarded_claims.remediation: Change line 198 to use a 2-tuple consistent with the deduplication scheme: advisor_key = (confirmed_by_model, "advisor").

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The literal code observation is accurate but the claimed mechanism and impact are both contradicted by the code. Line 188 builds `key = (model, role)` (2-tuple) and line 198 builds `advisor_key = (confirmed_by_model, None, "advisor")` (3-tuple) in the same `seen` set. However, the claim's core assertion -- that this 'breaks the deduplication logic entirely' because the 3-tuple 'will never match existing 2-tuples' -- is wrong: advisor keys are constructed consistently as 3-tuples every time, so 3-tuple-vs-3-tuple comparison works correctly. Two findings that share `confirmed_by_model = "opus"` both produce the identical key `("opus", None, "advisor")`; the second is found in `seen` and skipped. Advisor-to-advisor dedup therefore functions, and the claimed impact ('duplicate advisor entries with the same model may be added') is not reachable by the described path. The only way a duplicate advisor entry could arise is if an agent finding's derived role were literally the string 'advisor' (requiring `discovered_by == "agent:advisor"`) AND the same model string also appeared as some finding's `confirmed_by_model`. That is unreachable in this pipeline: /skill/scripts/provenance.py is the sole writer of `discovered_by` and emits only `tool:<adapter>` or `agent:<role>`; the only finding-emitting role templates are /skill/agents/panel-review.md (`agent:panel_review`) and /skill/agents/lens-sweep.md (`agent:lens_sweep`); and /skill/scripts/evidence.py `apply_verdict` writes `"agent:advisor"` into `confirmed_by`, never into `discovered_by`. Advisors emit verdicts, not findings, so `_role_from_discovered_by` can never return 'advisor'. The proposed remediation is harmless cosmetic tidying but changes no reachable output. Empirical confirmation from a real run: /docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-self-scan-report.json contains four findings with `confirmed_by_model: "opus"` (e.g. line 607) yet `meta.models_used` (lines 8-19) holds exactly two entries, lens_sweep and panel_review, with zero duplicates -- the opposite of the claimed symptom. Note for the auditor: those same lines do contain a real but *different* defect, which this claim misdiagnoses. The advisor block at lines 196-201 sits below the `if key in seen: continue` guard at lines 189-190, so `confirmed_by_model` is only ever inspected on the FIRST finding for a given (model, role) pair. In the self-scan run every advisor-confirmed finding was a non-first finding for its (model, role), so the advisor model was dropped from `models_used` entirely. discarded_claims.title: Inconsistent sys.path manipulation depth in dispatch.py
discarded_claims.description: dispatch.py adds only the current directory to sys.path (one os.path.dirname call), while all peer files (_run_adapter.py, run_tools.py, synthesize.py) add the parent directory (two os.path.dirname calls). This inconsistency could cause fragility if dispatch.py is later refactored to depend on scripts.* imports.
discarded_claims.impact: Inconsistent module import patterns can lead to import failures or confusion when the code structure changes or is maintained by others.
discarded_claims.remediation: Align sys.path manipulation in dispatch.py line 9 to use os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(...)) consistently with peer modules, or document why the different depth is intentional.
references: skill/scripts/dispatch.py:9-11 (one-dirname insert paired with bare `import depth_planner`/`import model_resolver`)
tests/test_synthesize.py:9,1086 (only skill/ on sys.path, then `import scripts.dispatch` -- proves the one-dirname insert is load-bearing)
skill/scripts/tools/base.py:9 and skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:11 (third, os.pardir-based sys.path form -- refutes a single two-dirname convention)

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The surface observation is true (dispatch.py line 9 uses one os.path.dirname, three peers use two), but the characterization as an inconsistency/fragility defect is wrong, and the proposed remediation would break the code. The sys.path depth in each module is functionally determined by that module's import style, not by an arbitrary convention. dispatch.py lines 10-11 do bare top-level imports (`import depth_planner`, `import model_resolver`); those modules live in skill/scripts/, so the ONE-dirname insert of skill/scripts/ is exactly what makes them resolve. The peers cited do package imports instead -- run_tools.py:12-13 `from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS`, synthesize.py:14-18 `import scripts.citations`, _run_adapter.py:12 `from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS` -- which require the PARENT dir (skill/) on the path, hence two dirnames. Both depths are correct and required for their respective import styles. Applying the stated remediation to dispatch.py line 9 would put skill/ on sys.path instead of skill/scripts/ and `import depth_planner` would raise ModuleNotFoundError. This is not hypothetical: tests/test_synthesize.py:9 puts only skill/ on sys.path and then line 1086 does `import scripts.dispatch as dispatch`. In that import path skill/scripts/ is on sys.path from no other source (Python only auto-adds the script dir for direct script execution, which this is not), so dispatch.py's own one-dirname insert is the sole reason its bare imports resolve. The remediation would break that test and every consumer of scripts.dispatch. The claim's premise that 'all peer files' use two dirnames is also false. Of the 12 peer modules in skill/scripts/, only three do the two-dirname insert; eight (depth_planner, model_resolver, citations, provenance, evidence, html_report, orchestrator, run_fixture_tests) perform no sys.path manipulation at all, and ingest_tools.py does scripts.* imports with no insert of its own, relying on the caller. Further, skill/scripts/tools/base.py:9 and skill/scripts/tools/sarif_utils.py:11 use a THIRD distinct form, `os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), os.pardir, os.pardir)` (os.pardir-based, non-abspath). So there is no single two-dirname convention that dispatch.py deviates from. Separately, the CWE-99 citation (Improper Control of Resource Identifiers / 'Resource Injection') is misapplied -- nothing here involves attacker-controlled resource identifiers -- and it is flagged verified:false. Note in fairness: the repo already tracks a general 'sys.path convention' cleanup as a known parked ledger item (docs/superpowers/2026-08-03-calibration-fixmes.md:105, 2026-08-04-issue-filing-handoff.md:52, specs/2026-08-03-tool-policy-enforcement-design.md:6,150), and the genuinely inconsistent cases are the tools/ os.pardir form and ingest_tools.py's missing insert -- not dispatch.py line 9, which is the one the claim targets and which is correct as written.

discarded_claims.title: model_resolver.py's 'WARNING:' stderr prefix diverges from the package's '<module>: ' convention

Every sibling module that emits similar tolerant-fallback stderr diagnostics prefixes with its own lowercase module name instead: citations.py's `"citations: ..."`, ingest_tools.py's `"ingest: ..."`, dispatch.py's `"dispatch: ..."`, evidence.py's `"evidence: ..."`, synthesize.py's `"synthesize: ..."`.

discarded_claims.title: Shell injection via unescaped fixture paths
discarded_claims.description: Fixture paths from the manifest are directly interpolated into a shell script string without escaping. An attacker-controlled manifest with paths containing shell metacharacters (quotes, semicolons, backticks) can break out of the intended if-statement context and execute arbitrary shell commands when the script is executed via `sh -c`.
discarded_claims.impact: An attacker who can modify the manifest.json file can execute arbitrary commands inside the Docker container, potentially compromising the build environment or exfiltrating data.
discarded_claims.remediation: Use shlex.quote() to escape each path before interpolating it into the shell script, or refactor to avoid shell script construction entirely by using subprocess with a list of arguments for each path check.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The syntactic pattern is quoted accurately: skill/scripts/run_fixture_tests.py:53-56 interpolates each fixture path into an f-string ('if [ -d "{p}" ]; then echo "PRESENT:{p}"; else echo "MISSING:{p}"; fi') with no escaping, and the joined string is handed to `sh -c` at line 52/57. Inside those double quotes a literal quote, backtick, or $(...) would execute. But no trust boundary is crossed, so the claimed vulnerability does not hold. (1) The input is not attacker-reachable: MANIFEST is a module-level constant at line 13, REPO_ROOT/tests/fixtures/manifest.json, derived from __file__ — it always resolves to panopticon's OWN repo file and never to a scan target. argparse in main() exposes only --tag, --rebuild and --test; there is no flag or env var to point the manifest elsewhere. (2) The values are static: all four `path` entries in tests/fixtures/manifest.json are committed constants (/opt/panopticon-fixtures/{railsgoat,WebGoat,AspGoat,vulnerable-rust}) containing no metacharacters, and a repo-wide grep for manifest.json across *.py shows the file is only ever read (line 96), never written or generated by any code path. (3) The precondition is self-defeating: an attacker who can modify manifest.json already has write access to the working tree, hence to run_fixture_tests.py itself and to Dockerfile.fixtures — which already executes arbitrary RUN commands and a `curl -sfL https://dot.net/... | bash` at line 16. Injection through the manifest therefore grants zero capability beyond what the stated precondition already implies. (4) Nothing automated reaches the sink: check_fixtures is called only from main() in the same file (no test or other module references it), .github/workflows/ci.yml runs only ruff and `pytest tests/ -q` on the runner, and no workflow in .github/ invokes run_fixture_tests.py or uses pull_request_target. DEVELOPMENT.md:79 documents it as a manually run local developer harness. discarded_claims.title: Missing edge case tests for render_prompt brace-escaping logic
discarded_claims.description: dispatch.py's render_prompt() (lines 151-176) implements two-step brace replacement using sentinel tokens to handle values containing brace syntax. However, test_dispatch.py does not include tests verifying that placeholder values containing '{...}' literal syntax pass through correctly and don't interfere with sentinel replacement.
discarded_claims.impact: If a prompt template has placeholder values like {'model':'x'} (e.g., from JSON config), the escaping logic might fail, leaving unresolved sentinels or corrupting the prompt.
discarded_claims.remediation: Add test cases that render prompts with placeholder values containing literal brace syntax, verify values pass through without sentinel corruption, and test deeply nested brace patterns.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: The claim's central factual assertion -- that test_dispatch.py lacks tests verifying placeholder values containing literal '{...}' syntax pass through without interfering with sentinel replacement -- is false. The repo contains exactly those tests, in the single test_dispatch.py that exists repo-wide (/Volumes/Mini Vault/untitled_folder/projects/panopticon/tests/test_dispatch.py; a repo-wide grep for render_prompt returns only this test file plus dispatch.py itself). (1) tests/test_dispatch.py:229-233, test_brace_safety_value_containing_placeholder_syntax, sets mapping['file_list'] = 'weird-{depth}-name.py' -- a value embedding a *live* placeholder token from the same mapping, the hardest case -- and asserts assertIn('weird-{depth}-name.py', p), i.e. it survives literally with no sentinel corruption. That is verbatim the test the claim says is missing. (2) tests/test_dispatch.py:276-305, TestRenderAdvisor.test_writes_one_prompt_per_entry, covers the claim's own hypothesized impact scenario (brace-laden JSON config values): the queue fixture embeds 'raw query with {code_context} text' in a finding description (line 283); render_advisor_prompts json.dumps that finding and feeds it to render_prompt('advisor.md', {'claim_json': claim}) (dispatch.py:345-346); the test then asserts assertIn('{code_context}', text) AND assertNotIn('{claim_json}', text) -- proving a brace-heavy JSON value containing a literal placeholder token renders through intact while the real placeholder is filled. (3) tests/test_dispatch.py:217-219 asserts no known placeholder token survives rendering (no unresolved sentinels/placeholders). (4) tests/test_dispatch.py:260-273 pins byte-exact golden renders for panel-review.md, lens-sweep.md and scout.md, so any sentinel leakage or corruption breaks the suite. Beyond the tests, the hypothesized failure mode is unreachable by construction: the sentinel is '\x00PANOPTICON%d\x00' (dispatch.py:171), NUL-delimited so no realistic value can collide; and the two passes are strictly ordered -- every '{tok}' is replaced with a sentinel in the first loop (line 173) before any value is substituted in the second (lines 174-175) -- so injected values are never re-scanned for placeholders and cannot interfere. PLACEHOLDER_RE = r'\{([a-z_]+)\}' (dispatch.py:79) also does not match JSON like {"model": "x"} (quotes/space/colon), so the claim's example is doubly inert. The only unaddressed remediation item, 'deeply nested brace patterns', exercises no distinct code path -- render_prompt does flat str.replace with no nesting-sensitive behavior -- and is not a defensible test gap. Claim rests on an unverified premise about test coverage that the repository refutes.

discarded_claims.description: html_report.py _escape() and _severity_class() (lines 172-174, 292-295) sanitize values for safe HTML insertion and CSS classes. test_html_report.py has basic escape tests (lines 64-66) but lacks comprehensive tests for control characters, very long strings, Unicode edge cases, and combinations of escape-required characters.
discarded_claims.impact: Sanitization edge cases might allow malformed HTML/CSS or display issues. While test_severity_class_sanitizes_input() exists, coverage for _escape() with combined entities or control characters is incomplete.
discarded_claims.remediation: Add parametrized tests covering all HTML entity combinations, Unicode high-value characters, strings >1000 chars, and repeated escape sequences.

provenance.confirmation_reasoning: Line citations are accurate: _escape is at skill/scripts/html_report.py:172-174 and _severity_class at :292-295, and tests/test_html_report.py:64-66 is the single direct _escape test. The literal predicate (no parametrized Unicode/control-char/>1000-char tests) is true, but the finding is rejected because the code contradicts its stated impact and its remediation has no defect-detection power. (1) _escape is a three-line pass-through: `return html.escape(str(value))`. The requested tests for 'Unicode high-value characters', 'strings >1000 chars' and 'control characters' would assert CPython stdlib behavior, not repository code; there is no branch, buffer, or truncation logic in the wrapper that could fail on length or codepoint. Notably html.escape deliberately does NOT escape control characters, so the suggested control-char test would assert pass-through, and control chars in an HTML text node are not an injection vector. (2) The security-relevant behaviors are already covered, and the claim's description omits the strongest existing test: test_title_escaped_once (tests/test_html_report.py:76-81) renders a `<script>` target through the full render() path and asserts `assertNotIn("&lt;", out)` — that is the genuine failure mode for an escape wrapper (double-escaping), already guarded. test_escape_escapes_html already exercises a combination of escape-required characters (`<`, `>`, `'`) in one string, which is the 'combined entities' case the claim says is missing. (3) The claimed CSS-malformation impact is impossible for _severity_class: `"".join(c for c in str(severity) if c.isalnum()).lower()` reduces input to [a-z0-9], so no input can produce malformed CSS or escape the quoted class attribute; test_severity_class_sanitizes_input (:422-426) already covers the injection case (`CRITICAL<script>` -> `sev-criticalscript`) and the empty-string edge case, which the claim itself concedes. (4) The CWE-79 / A03:2021-Injection citation is inapt: neither cited function has an XSS-capable path, and _escape uses html.escape with default quote=True across all 40 call sites in the module. Incidental note for the auditor, outside this claim's scope: _render_citation_quality (skill/scripts/html_report.py:325-327) interpolates `quality` into a class attribute as `f"<span class='cit-quality cit-{quality}'>"` with only `str(quality).lower()` applied — unlike the sibling _severity_class and the _render_provenance status_class at :315 which uses `re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9-]", "-", ...)` per an existing SEC-101 remediation. That is the actual unsanitized attribute interpolation in this file; TQ-005 points at the two functions that are correctly sanitized and tested rather than at that one.
